result:
You have never seen your own face. Not once, not truly. Everything you know about it arrives secondhand: the mirror's reversed image, the photograph's frozen flatness, the nose that looms perpetually at the bottom of your vision until your brain edits it out. Strangers on the street know your face more intimately than you do—they watch it move through real light, expressions blooming and fading in real time, while you sit at home reconstructing yourself from photographic evidence.

Maybe that explains the small jolt of strangeness when you find yourself in an unexpected photo. *Is that really me?* It is—and it's the only version anyone else has ever known. The face in your imagination is a patchwork assembled from bathroom mirrors and badly angled video calls, subtly wrong in ways no correction can fix.

There's comedy buried in all this. You spend your entire life hidden behind your face, operating it like elaborate machinery—a raised eyebrow here, a practiced smile there—then collecting secondhand reviews on how it landed. Everyone else serves as your cinematographer. Their memories archive every expression you've ever worn, ready to replay in rooms you'll never enter.

Some animals share the predicament. Elephants, magpies, and toddlers eventually pass the mirror test, which researchers treat as proof of self-awareness—as though recognizing your reflection settles anything. All it confirms is what we already suspected: you can spend decades commanding a face you will never directly witness, trusting everyone else to tell you what it looks like when it matters most.
